catalog_quote: Stress still needs to be investigated in greater detail. However, some preliminary findings shall be outlined here. Stress is free in the sense that its position cannot be predicted for any word from general phonological rules. Stress seems to be lexically conditioned. It may fall on the first syllable of bisyllabic words: bisyllabic word, 1st syllable stressed: "rE.ŋE ’woman’ "maŋ.ra ’money’ ... "la.ka ’v. dance’ "kpa.ra ’flying fox’ Note that in most of these examples, the first and the second syllable both lack a coda and are thus ’light’ syllables. In bisyllabic words, stress may also be on the second syllable, and this seems to be the case where at least the second syllable is closed and thus ’heavy’: bisyllabic word, 2nd syllable stressed: lak."lak ’v. dance (red)’ va."Pal ’banana’ Paŋ."sar ’person’ ... With trisyllabic words, stress is on the last syllable: ... trisyllabic word, …

new_statements.citation: François, Alexandre. 2005. Unraveling the history of the vowels of seventeen northern Vanuatu languages. Oceanic Linguistics 44(2): 443-504.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: lines 379-381 (printed p. 451, sec. 3.1 'Prosodic stress and vowel reduction') read: "The loss of word-²nal posttonic vowels explains why, in essentially all the lan-guages of the area, words are now systematically stressed on their ²nal rather than their penultimate syllable (contra Lynch 2000:77)." The preceding sentences (lines 368-378) confirm the historical part: protoforms 'systematically received primary stress on their penultimate syllable, and secondary stress every second syllable leftward'. Vera'a-specific pass…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For the seventeen Torres-Banks languages as a group (Vera'a among them), François states that after the loss of word-final unstressed vowels, stress now falls on the final syllable (historically the penult). He does not state a Vera'a-specific rule; his own Vera'a data (p. 464, Table 4 p. 476) show that Vera'a alone among the Vanua Lava languages retains a word-final echo vowel (Vf) that is unstressed and elidable phrase-medially, so a uniform 'final stress' reading cannot be projected onto Vera'a words that end in an echo vowel (stress would sit on the last full vowel, i.e. the penult of such words). An unpublished claim on Wikipedia (editor edit summary 2023-10-04: 'Vera'a and Mota have lost penult stress.. These are now stress-less lgs'; article sentence added 2023-11-11: 'There is no stress in Veraʼa') contradicts the area-level final-stress statement. The primary description (Schnell 2011/2010) could not be opened.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only historical: protoforms 'received primary stress on their penultimate syllable, and secondary stress every second syllable leftward' (p. 451); nothing synchronic for Vera'a.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedge 'essentially all the languages of the area'. Vera'a-specific caveat p. 464: 'This suggests that the final vowel Vf of Vera'a has a specific elidable status when (and only when) it proceeds from a posttonic [+low] V2 in a process of vowel reduction' (VRA 'ala 'clam' final /a/ contrasted with the 'final stressed' schwa of Lo-Toga); Table 4 p. 476 VRA: '[-sonorous] > Ø / [+sonorous] > Vf'. Wikipedia (uncited, editor-origin) says there is no stress in Vera'a at all. Note the text layer of the PDF renders the 'fi' ligature as '²'; 'final' restored in the quote.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, comparative-historical claim about citation forms; phrase-level effect noted: the Vera'a echo vowel is dropped phrase-medially (naka 'canoe' > nak susu, p. 464). No instrumental or synchronic prosodic description of Vera'a was found.
new_statements.identity_note: Vera'a [vra] was split off from 'Vatrata' [vlr] together with Lemerig [lrz] by ISO change request 2008-069; our earlier rosters carried it under the retired code vatr1237. François abbreviates it VRA. The Wikipedia editor's claim ('Vera'a and Mota have lost penult stress') also concerns Mota (mota1237). No dialect issue: the language is spoken in the single village of Vera'a on Vanua Lava.
